edges.description: Reproduces a systemic, partial (roughly 50%) complex I deficiency in both sexes, matching the partial rather than complete enzyme deficit inferred in patients.
edges.limitations: S55A is an engineered allele, not one of the human pathogenic variants (p.Gly8Arg, p.Arg37Ser, c.55C>T, p.Gly32Arg), so it models the consequence of MWFE dysfunction rather than any specific patient genotype. The phenotype is also dominated by metabolic and behavioural readouts rather than the Leigh syndrome or myoclonic epilepsy that define the human disease.

edges.description: The model develops age-dependent Purkinje neuron degeneration, giving a neurodegenerative phenotype, but this is a late cerebellar degeneration rather than the subacute necrotizing encephalomyelopathy or myoclonic epilepsy that define the human presentations.
edges.limitations: The neuropathology does not match the human disease in either distribution or tempo: Leigh syndrome involves basal ganglia and brainstem lesions with infantile or early childhood onset, whereas this model shows age-dependent Purkinje cell loss. No seizure phenotype corresponding to the human myoclonic epilepsy presentation is reported.

nodes.description: Two-dimensional blue native gel electrophoresis of patient fibroblasts shows reduced amounts of fully assembled complex I with no accumulation of lower-molecular-weight subcomplexes. That negative finding is the mechanistically informative one: an assembly pathway blocked at a defined intermediate would leave that intermediate behind, so its absence points to failure of assembly, destabilization of the assembled holoenzyme, or both, rather than a discrete arrest point.

nodes.description: Less intact complex I means less NADH oxidation and less electron delivery to ubiquinone, reducing proton pumping and oxidative phosphorylation capacity. NADH that cannot be reoxidized through the respiratory chain is instead consumed by cytosolic lactate dehydrogenase, which is why the biochemical signature is lactic acidosis and a raised lactate-to-pyruvate ratio. The deficiency is partial rather than complete — the mouse model of an equivalent allele shows roughly 50% residual activity — consistent with survival to presentation rather than embryonic lethality.

nodes.description: The clinical endpoint. Neurons and muscle are the tissues least able to tolerate reduced oxidative phosphorylation capacity, so the disease presents as encephalomyopathy: Leigh syndrome in one index patient, myoclonic epilepsy with developmental delay in the other, and muscular hypotonia with lactic acidosis in the affected heterozygous girl. Phenotypic variability between patients carrying different NDUFA1 alleles was noted from the outset.

nodes.description: NDUFA1 encodes MWFE, a small accessory (non-catalytic) subunit of complex I that is nonetheless essential for the holoenzyme to assemble and remain stable. Reported pathogenic alleles are missense — p.Gly8Arg and p.Arg37Ser hemizygously in the index males, c.55C>T identified later by exome sequencing, and p.Gly32Arg in an affected heterozygous female.

evidence.snippet: The resulting allele Ndufa1S55A introduced systemic serine-55-alanine (S55A) mutation within the MWFE protein, which is essential for Complex I assembly and stability.

genetic_context.description: Germline missense variants in the X-chromosomal NDUFA1 gene, hemizygous in affected males and heterozygous in the reported affected female.

nodes.description: A homologous-recombination knock-in introducing a point mutation in the 55th codon of Ndufa1, producing a systemic serine-55-alanine substitution in the MWFE protein. Described by its authors as the first genuine X-chromosome linked mouse model of systemic partial complex I deficiency.

Because NDUFA1 is X-linked, a heterozygous female is a mosaic of cells expressing either the wild-type or the mutant allele, and her phenotype depends on which allele is active in the affected tissue. In the reported affected girl, 72% of NDUFA1 mRNA in muscle carried the mutation and 74% of the active allele in that muscle was the paternally inherited one — skewing toward the mutant allele in the very tissue that was biochemically deficient. This is why heterozygous females cannot be assumed to be unaffected carriers, and it modifies the whole chain rather than sitting at one point in it.
